questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What decides the pressure at a point in a still fluid
questions.learningObjective: identify the variables that fix the pressure in a static fluid
questions.stem: A tank of water is given an odd shape, with a narrow arm on one side and a wide base below, and it is filled to a marked level. What sets the pressure at a point on the base?

options.text: The depth of that point below the free surface, and the density of the liquid
The volume of liquid above the point, since that mass presses down on it
options.misconception: believes the mass above a point sets its pressure

options.text: The width of the tank at the level of the point, which sets the load carried
options.misconception: believes the width of the vessel sets the pressure inside

options.text: The shape of the walls, since they push inward on the liquid under load
options.misconception: attributes the pressure to the shape of the container

questions.explanation: In a fluid at rest the pressure increase from the surface down to a depth is the weight per unit area of the column above, so only the vertical depth and the density enter, and the shape of the vessel is irrelevant. Taking the density of water as 1.00e3 kg per cubic metre and the acceleration due to gravity as 9.80 m per second squared, a point 12.0 m down sits at a gauge pressure of 1.18e5 Pa whether it lies under the wide base or the narrow arm. The reason is that a liquid cannot sustain a sideways stress, so the pressure of a deep column is felt sideways as well as downward.
questions.hint: Ask what the weight above a point does, and whether the walls change that.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What Pascal's principle states
questions.learningObjective: state the content of Pascal's principle
questions.stem: A sealed vessel of fluid is fitted with a small piston and connected by a pipe to a much larger piston. What does Pascal's principle say happens when the small one is pushed?

options.text: The pressure change appears at the large piston undiminished by the pipe
The pressure change at the large piston is smaller in proportion to its area
options.misconception: believes the pressure falls with the area it acts on

options.text: The force needed at the small piston rises with the square of the area ratio
options.misconception: invents a squared area relation for the required force

options.text: Nothing happens until the fluid is heated, since pressure needs a temperature rise
options.misconception: believes a pressure change requires heating

questions.explanation: Pascal's principle says a change in the pressure applied to a confined fluid is transmitted through the whole of it undiminished, which is what allows a small piston to move a large one. What the large piston gains in area it must lose in force, so with an area ratio of 50 the force needed falls by the same factor and a 1.0e5 N effort lifts 2.0e3 N of load. The pressure is the same on both pistons at every instant, and it is the common area that converts one into the other.
questions.hint: Ask what the fluid does to a pressure change applied to it.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Gauge pressure against absolute pressure
questions.learningObjective: distinguish gauge pressure from absolute pressure
questions.stem: A gauge on a water pipe reads 3.0e5 Pa while water is flowing. What is the absolute pressure at that point, and why does the distinction matter?

options.text: About 4.0e5 Pa, since the ambient pressure of roughly 1.0e5 Pa must be added
About 2.0e5 Pa, since the ambient pressure must be subtracted from the gauge
options.misconception: subtracts the ambient pressure instead of adding it

options.text: Exactly 3.0e5 Pa, since a gauge already measures against a vacuum
options.misconception: believes a mechanical gauge reads against a vacuum

options.text: About 3.0e5 Pa, since the ambient pressure acts equally on both sides of the metal
options.misconception: assumes the ambient contribution cancels inside the gauge

questions.explanation: A mechanical gauge reads the difference between the pressure of the fluid and the pressure of the atmosphere around its case, so the absolute value is the gauge reading plus the ambient value, 3.0e5 Pa plus 1.0e5 Pa, which is about 4.0e5 Pa. The difference is not academic: cavitation and boiling depend on the absolute pressure, because a liquid boils when its own vapour pressure is reached, and that judgement needs the total and not the excess. A gauge that reads zero is therefore not a vacuum, it is simply at atmospheric pressure.
questions.hint: Ask what the case of the gauge is exposed to on its outside face.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What Archimedes' principle states
questions.learningObjective: state the content of Archimedes' principle
questions.stem: An object is lowered into water and released, and the water exerts an upward force on it. According to Archimedes' principle, what sets the size of that force?

options.text: The weight of the water the object displaces, which is found from the displaced volume
The weight of the object itself, since the water supports whatever is placed in it
options.misconception: believes the upthrust equals the weight of the immersed body

options.text: The volume of the whole tank of water, since all of it presses upward at once
options.misconception: uses the total liquid volume instead of the displaced part

options.text: The depth of the object below the surface, since deeper water presses harder
options.misconception: makes the upthrust depend on immersion depth

questions.explanation: The upward force a fluid exerts on a body equals the weight of the fluid that the body displaces, and since the weight of a volume of fluid is its density times its volume times the acceleration due to gravity, the upthrust on 2.0e-3 cubic metres of water is 1.00e3 times 2.0e-3 times 9.80, which is 19.6 N. The force does not depend on how deep the object is, because the pressure increase with depth and the decrease over the sides of the body exactly cancel, which is why a fully submerged object feels the same lift at any depth.
questions.hint: Ask what the displaced fluid would weigh if it were in the vessel instead.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Why a dense object sinks and a less dense one floats
questions.learningObjective: relate floatation to the densities of the body and the fluid
questions.stem: A block of density 800 kg per cubic metre is placed in water of density 1.00e3 kg per cubic metre. What happens to it, and what fraction of it ends up below the surface?

options.text: It floats with 0.80 of its volume submerged, because that is the displaced fraction
It sinks, because it is lighter than the water and so cannot be held up
options.misconception: reverses the rule that the denser material sinks

options.text: It floats with 0.20 of its volume submerged, since 0.20 of it is lighter than water
options.misconception: reports the unsubmerged fraction as the submerged one

options.text: It floats with 0.50 submerged, because a floating body always sits half in the liquid
options.misconception: assumes every floating body is half submerged

questions.explanation: A floating body settles where the upthrust equals its weight, and the upthrust is the weight of the displaced fluid, so the submerged fraction is the ratio of the densities, 800 divided by 1.00e3, which is 0.80. The remaining 0.20 stands clear of the surface, and that is the fraction a lighter material would show. Density is the whole story, which is why ice floats on water while a wooden block of the same shape does not, and why a ship floats higher in salt water than in fresh.
questions.hint: Set the weight of the displaced water equal to the weight of the block.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: The continuity condition for a steady flow
questions.learningObjective: state the continuity relation and the assumption behind it
questions.stem: A liquid flows steadily through a pipe that changes in cross-section, and the flow rate is measured in cubic metres per second. How do the speed and the area vary along the pipe?

options.text: Their product is constant, since the same volume passes each section each second
Their sum is constant, since the total flow along the pipe is fixed
options.misconception: adds speed and area where their product is fixed

options.text: The speed is constant, since a steady flow cannot accelerate along its path
options.misconception: believes steady flow means uniform speed everywhere

options.text: The speed varies with the square of the area, following a squared relation
options.misconception: squares the area where a simple quotient is required

questions.explanation: In a steady flow the amount of liquid crossing any section per second is the same, since nothing accumulates anywhere along the pipe, and that amount is the section area times the mean speed through it. So the product of area and speed is constant, and where the pipe narrows the speed rises in proportion, so halving the area doubles the speed. The relation assumes the liquid is effectively incompressible, which water very nearly is, and it makes no statement about pressure, which is where the other half of the story enters.
questions.hint: Ask how much liquid passes a given cross-section each second.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What the Bernoulli expression holds constant
questions.learningObjective: interpret the terms of the Bernoulli expression
questions.stem: Water flows steadily along a pipe that changes in height and cross-section. What does the Bernoulli expression say stays the same from one point to the next?

options.text: The pressure term plus the kinetic term plus the height term, along a streamline
The pressure alone, since the other two terms describe the pipe rather than the fluid
options.misconception: believes pressure is constant along a streamline

options.text: The kinetic term alone, since only the speed changes as the fluid moves
options.misconception: isolates one term of a three-term expression

options.text: The total energy of the fluid, since energy is conserved everywhere in a fluid
options.misconception: reads the relation as conservation of total energy

questions.explanation: Bernoulli's expression says that along a streamline the sum of the pressure, the kinetic energy per unit volume and the potential energy per unit volume does not change, each term being measured at the same point. The statement assumes a steady, incompressible, non-viscous flow, so in a real pipe the sum falls as friction removes energy, and the fall is a measure of the losses. The relation is what links the three measurable quantities, since a faster stream must sit at a lower pressure, which is the whole of the atomiser and the aerofoil argument.
questions.hint: Ask which quantities appear together in the expression, and along what line.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Why a narrowing pipe speeds the flow up
questions.learningObjective: connect continuity and the pressure change in a constriction
questions.stem: A pipe narrows smoothly and a small tube is tapped into the narrow part. Compared with the wide part, what does the narrow part show at the tap?

options.text: A faster flow and a lower pressure, since the same volume passes less area
A slower flow and a lower pressure, since the narrow part resists the passage
options.misconception: believes a restriction slows the flow and raises the pressure

options.text: A faster flow and a higher pressure, since the pump drives harder through a narrow part
options.misconception: assumes a constriction raises the pressure in a moving fluid

options.text: The same flow and a lower pressure, since only the area of the pipe has changed
options.misconception: assumes continuity fails when the cross-section changes

questions.explanation: Continuity forces the speed up where the area is smaller, since the same volume per second has to pass through every section, and the work done in accelerating that liquid comes out of the pressure, so the pressure falls. Together the two effects make the constriction a suction point, and a tube tapped there draws liquid upwards when the fall in pressure exceeds the weight of the column it has to lift. This is the working principle of a carburettor, a pressure atomiser and a venturi flow meter, all of which are the same arrangement used for different purposes.
questions.hint: Ask which way continuity pushes the speed, and where the energy for that comes from.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What viscosity does to flow through a pipe
questions.learningObjective: describe the effect of viscosity on a pressure-driven flow
questions.stem: A liquid is pushed through a narrow horizontal tube by a difference in pressure between its ends. Which statement about viscosity is correct?

options.text: It resists the motion, so the flow rate is set by viscosity as well as by geometry
It has no effect, since a fluid in steady flow cannot resist being pushed
options.misconception: believes a steady fluid has no internal friction

options.text: It speeds the flow, since sticky molecules help the liquid along the tube
options.misconception: treats viscosity as a driving force rather than a brake

options.text: It sets the direction of the flow, deciding which end the liquid leaves by
options.misconception: assigns a directional role to a resistive property

questions.explanation: Viscosity is the internal friction of a fluid: layers slide past one another more slowly the closer they are to the wall, and the shear forces they exert must be supplied by the pressure difference that drives the flow. The result is that the flow rate is proportional to the pressure difference and inversely proportional to the viscosity, and that a more viscous liquid needs a larger driving pressure for the same delivery. For a given tube the dependence is very steep, with the rate going as the fourth power of the radius, which is why a small change of bore makes a large difference to a flow.
questions.hint: Ask what must be supplied to keep the layers of fluid sliding past one another.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Terminal speed as a balance of two forces
questions.learningObjective: explain why a falling object reaches a steady speed
questions.stem: A small sphere dropped into a viscous liquid falls steadily after a short time instead of speeding up without limit. What is happening to the forces on it?

options.text: The upward drag has grown until it matches the weight less the upthrust
The weight has fallen to match the drag, because the sphere is becoming lighter
options.misconception: believes a falling body loses mass as it descends

options.text: The drag has stopped changing, so the net force is zero at any speed above the first
options.misconception: assumes a constant drag force rather than a speed-dependent one

options.text: The upthrust has grown with depth until it balances the weight exactly
options.misconception: believes the upthrust increases with depth

questions.explanation: A body falling in a fluid has three forces on it: its weight down, the upthrust up, and a drag that grows as the speed rises, so the downward drive is fixed while the upward resistance climbs. When the two upward forces together equal the weight, the acceleration is zero and the speed stays at that value, which is the terminal speed. The drag depends on the speed rather than being constant, so a body entering a liquid at high speed slows down towards a lower terminal value, and a small sphere reaches it after a very short transient.
questions.hint: Ask which of the three forces on the body changes as it gathers speed.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What surface tension is
questions.learningObjective: describe surface tension as a surface effect with a measurable size
questions.stem: A drop of water on a plate spreads into a flattened drop rather than sitting as a sphere, and a needle floats on a water surface. What property of the liquid does this show?

options.text: The surface behaves as a stretched skin, with a tension that also shows on solids
The liquid has an internal friction that makes it spread slowly over any surface
options.misconception: confuses the surface effect with the internal viscosity

options.text: The liquid is denser at the surface, so the drop sinks until it flattens
options.misconception: explains a surface effect by a density difference inside the liquid

options.text: The plate is greasy, which is what stops the drop from taking a spherical shape
options.misconception: blames the container instead of the liquid surface

questions.explanation: Surface tension is the effect that makes a liquid surface behave like a stretched membrane, arising because molecules at the surface have fewer neighbours than those inside and so sit at a higher energy. It is measured as a force per unit length, and for water in air it is about 0.073 N per metre, which is why a steel needle can float on it and why water climbs a narrow tube. The same effect sets the shape of a drop, which is spherical in free air and flattened on a surface, because the surface tries to occupy as little area as it can for a given volume.
questions.hint: Ask what the molecules at the surface of a liquid have fewer of than those inside.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What a manometer compares
questions.learningObjective: state what a manometer measures and how it is read
questions.stem: A U-shaped tube partly filled with a heavy liquid has one limb connected to a gas pipe and the other left open to the air. What does the difference in level between the two limbs tell you?

options.text: The excess of the gas pressure over the atmospheric pressure, set by the height difference
The absolute pressure of the gas, since the open limb removes the atmospheric term
options.misconception: believes the open limb cancels rather than supplies the ambient

options.text: The temperature of the gas, since a pressure difference implies a temperature change
options.misconception: reads a pressure difference as a temperature measurement

options.text: The mass of gas in the pipe, since volume and pressure fix the mass together
options.misconception: infers a mass from a pressure reading alone

questions.explanation: The heavy liquid stands at different heights in the two limbs because the pressure at the bottom of each limb must be the same, and the difference in levels is what balances the difference between the gas pressure and the atmospheric pressure on the open side. So the reading is a gauge pressure, obtained by multiplying the height difference by the density of the manometer liquid and the acceleration due to gravity, and it is the excess rather than the absolute value. That is why such a gauge must be corrected for the weather, since the atmospheric side of the difference changes from day to day.
questions.hint: Ask why the liquid levels differ at all, and what the open limb is exposed to.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Why a dam is built thicker at the base
questions.learningObjective: reason from the growth of pressure with depth to a structural conclusion
questions.stem: A dam 30.0 m high is designed with a much thicker base than crest, and the water it holds is of density 1.00e3 kg per cubic metre. What reasoning leads to that shape?

options.text: The pressure grows with depth, so the deepest part of the face must resist the largest load
The water is deepest at the base, so the base carries the largest volume of liquid
options.misconception: reasons from the volume of water to the structural load

options.text: The base carries the whole weight of the water, which the crest does not have to hold
options.misconception: treats a hydrostatic load as the weight of the water above

options.text: The crest is exposed to wind, so the base is thickened to carry the greater of the two forces
options.misconception: invokes wind loading where the water load is the design case

questions.explanation: Pressure in a still liquid increases linearly with depth, so a face 30.0 m deep sees a gauge pressure of 2.94e5 Pa while the same face at 3.0 m down sees 2.94e4 Pa, a factor of ten less, and the total force on a face grows with the square of the depth. A wall of constant thickness would therefore be badly under-strength at the bottom and wastefully strong at the top, which is exactly the reverse of what a designer wants. Tapering the section to match the pressure profile lets the same quantity of material do the job everywhere along the face.
questions.hint: Ask how the pressure compares at one tenth of the depth and at full depth.

questions.topic: Why a ship's bow is raked forward
questions.learningObjective: reason from pressure differences to the shape of a hull
questions.stem: The underwater bow of a moving ship slopes forward rather than standing vertical, and a thin foil rises steeply out of the water. What common effect do both shapes exploit?

options.text: A tilted surface converts a pressure difference between its two faces into a force
A vertical surface would split the hull, so the rake is a structural necessity alone
options.misconception: ignores the flow effect in favour of structure alone

options.text: The rake keeps the bow clear of waves, which would otherwise push the ship down
options.misconception: explains a submerged shape by wave action alone

options.text: The rake reduces the upthrust so that the ship sits deeper in the water
options.misconception: confuses a change of shape with a change of displaced volume

questions.explanation: A surface inclined to the flow meets a region of differing pressure on its two sides, and the resultant of those pressures is a force roughly normal to the surface, which has a component along the direction of travel. That is the whole of the principle behind the raked bow of a ship, behind the camber of a bridge underside and behind the rise of a foil in water. It works because pressure always pushes normally on a surface, so tilting the surface tilts the force, and the upthrust on the tilted face acquires a forward component that the pressure difference has paid for.

questions.topic: Why equal masses of different sizes behave differently in a fluid
questions.learningObjective: reason from displaced volume to the behaviour of objects in a fluid
questions.stem: A coin and a paperclip of the same mass are dropped into a beaker of water, and the coin sinks while the paperclip floats briefly. What accounts for the difference?

options.text: The coin is denser, so it displaces less water for its weight and the upthrust wins
The paperclip is hollow, so the water cannot get inside it and push it down
options.misconception: attributes the result to a trapped rather than to a displaced volume

options.text: The coin is heavier, since the two were only assumed to have the same mass
options.misconception: reverses the premise that the masses are equal

options.text: The paperclip is slower, so the water reaches it later and holds it up for longer
options.misconception: explains a floatation difference by arrival time at the surface

questions.explanation: Equal mass means equal weight, but the upthrust depends on the volume of fluid displaced and not at all on the mass of the object, so the two are compared by density. This is the same comparison that decides whether a person floats, and the reason an object can be made to float by changing its shape without changing its mass at all.
questions.hint: Ask which quantity the upthrust actually depends on.

questions.topic: Why a floating body sits lower in salt water than in fresh
questions.learningObjective: reason from the density of the fluid to the submerged fraction
questions.stem: A boat whose hull has an effective density of 700 kg per cubic metre is moved from fresh water of density 1.00e3 to salt water of density 1.03e3 kg per cubic metre. What happens to the boat and why?

It sinks, because salt water is denser and so pushes harder on the hull
options.misconception: believes a denser fluid exerts more total upward force

options.text: It rises, because salt water is more viscous and so supports the hull better

The reasoning is identical for a person in a pool and in the sea, and it is why a body is easier to support in a dense fluid even though nothing about the fluid is pushing harder overall.

questions.topic: Pressure at depth in water

questions.stem: An open tank of water of density 1.00e3 kg per cubic metre stands 12.0 m deep. Taking the acceleration due to gravity as 9.80 m per second squared, what is the gauge pressure at the bottom in pascals?
questions.explanation: The gauge pressure at a depth is the density times the acceleration due to gravity times the depth, so p equals 1.00e3 times 9.80 times 12.0, which is 1.176e5 Pa, or 1.18e5 Pa to three significant figures. The check that the units are right is that dividing the pressure by the product of the density and gravity returns 12.0 m exactly, which is the depth that went in. The same calculation for a 10.3 m column gives 1.01e5 Pa, which is the figure usually quoted for normal atmospheric pressure.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Why a dam is thicker at its base than at its crest
questions.learningObjective: explain the structural consequence of the growth of pressure with depth
questions.stem: Explain in your own words why a water dam is made far thicker at the bottom than at the top, and state the two reasons a constant-thickness wall could not work.

answer.exemplar: The pressure of a still liquid grows linearly with depth, because each layer has to support the weight of everything above it, so a face 30.0 m down is pressed at 2.94e5 pascals while the same face 3.0 m down is pressed at 2.94e4. The total force on a face is that pressure integrated over the face, and since the pressure is greatest where the face is deepest, the resultant is concentrated at the bottom of the wall, at two thirds of the depth rather than at the middle. A wall of constant thickness would then be many times stronger than it needed to be at the crest, where the load is small, and dangerously weak at the base, where the load is large, and it would fail in tension on the water face at the foot long before the upper part was doing any work at all. Tapering the section to follow the pressure profile spends the material where the load is. The second reason is that the water exerts a horizontal thrust as well as a vertical one, since pressure acts in every direction, and that thrust tries to slide the base of the dam forwards, which is why a dam is also keyed into its foundation and not merely rested on it.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Why a wing carries a load in a moving stream
questions.learningObjective: explain the pressure difference that produces lift on an aerofoil
questions.stem: Explain how a wing in a moving stream of air can carry a load, and state the pressure difference and the size of the force for air of density 1.2 kg per cubic metre at 30 m per second over the wing and 35 m per second beneath it.

answer.exemplar: A fluid in motion carries energy as well as pressure, and the Bernoulli expression says that along a streamline the sum of the pressure, the kinetic energy per unit volume and the potential energy per unit volume is fixed, so wherever the flow is quicker the pressure must be lower. Over the top of a wing the flow is quicker than beneath it, so the pressure beneath is the higher of the two, and the difference acts over the whole underside as an upward force. With the given speeds the difference is half the density times the difference of the squares, that is 0.6 times 1225 minus 900, which is 195 pascals, and over a wing of 20 square metres that is a force of the order of 4000 newtons, which is enough to hold a light aeroplane up. A second contribution comes from the wing being inclined, since pressure acts normal to a surface and tilting the surface tilts the resultant so that part of it points upwards. Neither mechanism is a suction, and both are paid for by the small deficit in pressure and energy around the wing, which is why a stalled or a very low speed wing stops producing lift altogether.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Why a chimney draws
questions.learningObjective: explain the density difference that produces a draught
questions.stem: Explain in your own words why warm air in a 3.0 m chimney rises and draws smoke from a fire when the flue is shorter than the outdoor column of cold air it is connected to.

answer.exemplar: The driving force is a difference of density between two columns of air that stand side by side and are joined at the bottom, which is a liquid of low density obeying the same rules as water. Cold outdoor air of density 1.2 kg per cubic metre presses down on the top of the flue with a pressure set by the full height of the outdoor column, while the warm air inside the chimney, say 1.0 kg per cubic metre, presses down with a pressure set by its own column over 3.0 m, and since the outdoor air is both denser and standing higher, the pressure difference at the base is about 5.9 pascals in favour of the cold side. That difference pushes air up the flue, and the resulting speed, which follows from half the density times the speed squared being the pressure difference, is about 3.4 m per second, enough to carry smoke and combustion products out of the room. The reason the effect is weak is that the densities involved are so similar, and that is exactly why a flue works far better when it is tall, since the driving pressure grows with the difference in the two heights rather than with the height of the chimney alone.

questions.topic: Why the surface of a flowing stream tilts in a bend
questions.learningObjective: explain the shape of a free surface in a curved open channel
questions.stem: Explain why the free surface of water running round a bend is higher on the outside of the bend than on the inside, and give the size of the difference for a speed of 10 m per second in water with the acceleration due to gravity as 9.80 m per second squared.

answer.exemplar: A free surface is level only where the fluid is at rest or is moving in a straight line, because a level surface is one on which the pressure at every point is the same atmospheric value. In a bend the fluid on the outside of the curve has to follow a longer path at the same average speed, so by continuity it is moving faster there, and the Bernoulli expression says that the faster stream is the one at lower pressure. Since the surface of the stream is free, that lower pressure shows itself as a surface that stands higher, and the excess height is the speed head, half the speed squared divided by the acceleration due to gravity, which for 10 m per second is 100 over 19.6, that is 5.1 m. It is the same statement that a racing cyclist leans into a turn to avoid being thrown outwards, and it is the reason a badly designed bend in a canal throws its water against the outer bank and erodes it.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Why viscosity is negligible in air and decisive in a lubricant
questions.learningObjective: explain the role of viscosity in flows of very different densities
questions.stem: Explain why the viscosity of air is normally left out of the equations for a flying aeroplane but must be included for oil inside a bearing, and give the ratio of the two viscosities.

answer.exemplar: Viscosity only matters where the fluid has to be sheared, and how much shear there is depends on how tightly the fluid is packed and how fast it is being asked to move relative to its surroundings. Air is very sparse, so the number of molecules in a given volume is tiny and the shear forces between neighbouring layers are correspondingly weak, which is why the air in the path of a wing is treated as an ideal fluid whose energy and pressure terms simply rearrange. Oil between the surfaces of a bearing is a different matter, because it is a dense, closely packed liquid in continuous contact with two surfaces that are moving relative to each other, and the shear in the thin film there is the whole of the mechanism by which the load is carried and the friction is reduced. The two viscosities are about 1.8e-3 and 1.0e-3 pascal seconds for air and water respectively, so water is roughly fifty-six times as viscous as air, and an oil chosen for a bearing is typically many hundreds of times more viscous than air again.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Checking a flow rate against its quoted figure
questions.learningObjective: order the steps of a power rating check in a fluid circuit
questions.stem: Four statements describe how the flow rate of a small tube is checked against the figure its maker quotes. Put them in the order in which they occur, earliest first.

options.text: The measured 2.45e-4 cubic metres per second is compared with the 2.5e-4 on the data sheet
A pressure difference of 1.0e3 pascals is set across the tube and held steady while the reading is taken
The tube is connected between a reservoir and a collection vessel with a valve for adjusting the head
The difference is judged against the tolerance and against the temperature of the liquid during the test

questions.explanation: The apparatus has to exist before a driving pressure can be applied, so the tube is first connected between a reservoir, which sets the head, and a collection vessel, which catches the discharge. The valve then allows the pressure difference to be set at 1.0e3 pascals and held there, since the flow rate is the quantity being measured and it will not stay constant if the head drifts as the reservoir empties. Only then is a judgement made about the deviation from the quoted figure, because the measured value differs from the data sheet by about two percent, and viscosity falls by several tenths of a percent for each kelvin of temperature rise, so the temperature of the liquid has to be part of that judgement.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be connected before any pressure can be applied to the tube.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Verifying the continuity relation at two pipe areas
questions.learningObjective: order the steps of a two-point continuity measurement
questions.stem: Four statements describe how the continuity relation is checked on a pipe that narrows from 4.0e-4 to 1.0e-4 square metres. Put them in the order in which they occur, earliest first.

options.text: The two values of area times speed are compared and found to agree within the reading accuracy
The two cross-sections are measured and the narrow one is confirmed to be one quarter of the wide one
The flow is set running and the speed is measured in each section with a timed float or a meter
The result is recorded as a check on the steady state of the flow, since drift would spoil the comparison

questions.explanation: The geometry comes first, since the prediction depends on the ratio of the two areas and a measurement of those areas is what makes the comparison a test rather than a tautology. The flow is then established and the speed measured in each section, and for a wide section of 4.0e-4 square metres at 3.0 m per second the product is 1.2e-3 cubic metres per second, which the narrow section at 12 m per second must reproduce. Only after the two products have been compared does the steady state of the flow become the thing worth recording, since a drifting flow would make the two measurements refer to different instants and the agreement would be meaningless.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be known about the pipe before any prediction can be tested.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Deciding whether a pipe flow is orderly
questions.learningObjective: order the steps of a check on the character of a pipe flow
questions.stem: Four statements describe how a working pipe is checked to see whether its flow is orderly. Put them in the order in which they occur, earliest first.

options.text: The flow rate is recorded at each of several driving pressures to see if it stays proportional
The bore of the pipe and the viscosity of the liquid are measured or looked up
A dimensionless group is formed from the bore, the speed, the density and the viscosity
The conclusion is recorded together with the margin of error on the group, which sets the confidence

questions.explanation: The quantities that enter the group have to be known before the group can be formed, so the bore and the viscosity are measured or taken from a data sheet first, and the speed follows from the running flow. The comparison that decides the matter is then made by watching whether the flow rate stays in proportion to the driving pressure as that pressure is raised, because a proportional response is the mark of an orderly flow and a response that outgrows the pressure is the mark of a chaotic one. Only after both pieces of evidence exist does the conclusion get written down, and it is written with its uncertainty, since a value of the group near the boundary could be classified either way.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be measured before a dimensionless group can be formed at all.
